d8cd90eb2ec3e6fd: You can also check window placement with a simple relationship: compare the gap between the windows with the distances from each window to the left and right wall edges. 2712817588961b71: Prepare a black-and-white silhouette or flat-color image you have permission to use, such as a black leaf on white. 9cbd33c193e355e0: Use a different set of criteria for a multicolor photo: the result is a graphic representation with colors consolidated. d9694b28459aa34b: If lines in the original are faint, broken, or accompanied by paper texture, generated paths may contain both gaps and specks. db796bb667ee94ae: For a black-and-white silhouette, start with monochrome processing. The threshold is not a 'higher means clearer' slider; it changes what is retained and discarded.
ed3f47de2a6cd1d9: Not necessarily. Noise and fine texture also increase the path count. What matters is whether the contour expresses the intended shape, remains easy to edit, and reads clearly at the final size.

7caec60934bcaff9: This exercise expresses only 'mountain'; do not add a sun, river, houses, and explanatory text at the same time. 8eff54ab525ac9f2: Final checks and two output formats
9fb57a9b925021af: A white object differs from a transparent hole. On a dark background, white remains white. Decide whether to retain white or use an actual contour structure according to the intended use, and check the transparent output.
aa6be50f8cb717a2: Use alignment to establish a centered baseline, then examine visual weight. A mountain is pointed at the top and broad at the bottom, so mathematical centering may not look most stable. Make small vertical adjustments in a copy and compare which feels better. ae314f7b678560ed: Make geometric and visual centers work together
b02eb71e90196e63: Export a transparent PNG for common display uses, then an SVG for continued use of the paths. A general exercise does not automatically become a validated brand mark.
b75be671cca8c6ac: Design negative space together with the solid regions. A narrow gap between peaks may look attractive when large but disappear when reduced. bc2b80c6295af82b: Temporarily remove the secondary peak and compare which is clearer: one peak or two. Use the result to decide whether to retain the second object.
c02f4fad43ca608e: Should a small icon always be as simple as possible?
c7644254130f9520: Consider a simple light snowcap below the summit or a strip of negative space suggesting a facet. e72a719c163dced8: Use the silhouette to judge whether the icon is overdesigned
ed0763676c64b300: Simplicity usually helps, but excessive reduction can remove identifying features. Keep the contours and spaces that best express the subject, and remove details that cannot serve a purpose at the target size.
f54b94218d74d01c: Finally, compare visual area. Of two icons with equally sized bounding boxes, a solid mountain often feels heavier than a thin outline mountain. If they will appear alongside other icons, aim for visual balance across the set rather than forcing every shape to fill exactly the same bounds. Make slight size adjustments where necessary while retaining a clearly consistent style.
f61860906a2f1a92: Use the pen to draw a larger triangular peak, then a slightly shorter peak beside it. The peaks need not be perfectly symmetrical, but their hierarchy should be clear. Use only solid fills for now so gradients do not conceal the silhouette relationship. If their intersection becomes complicated, simplify the placement before continuing.
f666488203ac86c8: For a solid silhouette, express detail mainly through color regions and negative space. For a line icon, establish consistent stroke widths and endpoint styles. 0e2f12cc44f9e534: The pen creates paths made of anchor points and curve segments; it does not fill a region with many pixels. Nodes determine where the contour passes, while handles affect the direction and curvature as a curve approaches or leaves a node. The goal is to learn to observe curves, not to reproduce every detail of a natural plant on the first attempt.

5a79a8e24762decd: Do more nodes always mean greater precision?
7194582ed9bdb821: Understand what the pen does first
76d76de2833518c5: At a smooth turn, create handles with the pen's curve operation and observe how the arcs on either side change. Longer handles generally pull the nearby curve farther from a straight line, but length alone does not determine the overall shape; direction matters just as much. If the leaf develops a bulge, shorten the relevant handle and compare before immediately adding three nodes around it. You can finish a rough path first, then refine it in node editing.
79d3b73c8c314a37: If the right edge of the leaf makes only one gentle bend from top to bottom, try expressing it with the neighboring main nodes and their handles. Add a node only when the target contour genuinely has a second distinct bend. This differs from saying 'fewer nodes are always better': complex contours need enough nodes, but each should have a job. When finished, follow the contour and identify the shape change associated with every node. Recheck nodes for which you cannot identify a purpose.
7d37481ffe6ce625: No. More nodes can describe complex contours, but they also make local waviness and difficult-to-maintain shapes more likely. Start with a few nodes for the major turns and add more only when the existing curves cannot express the target.
7e31caf1c0f616d9: In an empty area, use the pen to create three corner points in order and return to the start to close a triangle. Observe the node order and how the final segment connects. Undo the latest step if you make a mistake instead of repeatedly clicking the same position and creating indistinguishable overlapping nodes. Closed paths suit filled shapes such as leaves; open paths suit single branches. A fill that appears to seal a contour does not mean the path has been properly closed.

aa39ff4751090629: Judge whether the silhouette looks natural at its normal display size, then zoom in to inspect the tip, bottom join, and side curves. adc884644daaf9b8: That cannot be promised. The pen is useful for reinterpreting contours and color regions; it does not automatically recover every texture in a photo. Decide which structures to retain before choosing manual paths or image vectorization.
